title: The only gift
hook: the only true gift is a portion of yourself (Gifts, 1844)

segments.voice: Yesterday, on friendship: Emerson's test that a friend is a person with whom I may be sincere. Your line was sincere. Who got to think aloud, you or your friend? Day one thousand two hundred four.

It's late, the birthday is tomorrow, and the shopping site promises it can still arrive in time. A candle. A nice mug. A gift card tucked into a bright envelope. Click, done, crisis over. Nothing wrong with any of it, and plenty of people are glad to get a gift card. But Emerson wrote a short essay called Gifts, and in it he sets a higher bar, with one blunt sentence about jewelry that can stop a reader short. Today, what he thought a real gift is.
screen: `LATE NIGHT, BIRTHDAY TOMORROW.` → `CLICK, DONE.` → `A HIGHER BAR.`

segments.voice: First, the blunt sentence. Emerson writes: "Rings and other jewels are not gifts, but apologies for gifts. The only gift is a portion of thyself." An apology for a gift. As if the bought thing says, sorry, I couldn't give you anything of me, so here's this instead. Second, what a portion of yourself looks like. Emerson gives a list. The poet brings a poem. The shepherd brings a lamb. The farmer brings his corn, the painter his picture, and a girl brings a handkerchief she sewed herself. Each one gives what passed through their own hands and life. The value isn't the price. It's that some of the giver is in it. Third, he isn't a scold about it. In the same essay he calls flowers and fruits fit presents, and he admits that giving and receiving are awkward, tangled things. The point isn't to never buy anything. It's to notice the difference between a present that carries you and one that only stands in for you. Fourth, the week's thread. This week Emerson asked us to hold self and others together, to watch what comes back, to feel contained in something larger, to draw another circle, to act with enthusiasm, to be sincere with a friend. Today, a gift. Read side by side, they share a thread, the same request in different rooms: the real thing, not a stand-in. A sincere word instead of a polished one. A whole effort instead of a half one. A portion of yourself instead of an apology for one.
screen: `APOLOGIES FOR GIFTS.` · `THE POET BRINGS HIS POEM.` · `FLOWERS AND FRUITS ARE FINE.` · `THE WEEK'S THREAD: THE REAL THING.` · then, large: `THE ONLY GIFT IS A PORTION OF THYSELF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan something you made, to give away. Settle, and breathe. Let one person come to mind, someone who could use a small kindness this week. Then ask what you could make for them. Not buy. Make. A short note in your own handwriting. A meal. A song you've picked out and why. A photo you took, printed. A repair. Something small enough to finish this week. Picture handing it over. The bell holds the time.
The only gift. Emerson's line from Gifts: rings and jewels are apologies for gifts, and the only gift is a portion of yourself. Today's word.
Your line: a portion of myself. Start the thing you pictured today, even just the first few lines of the note, and give it this week. Day one thousand two hundred four.

howItsDone: Readers who take Emerson's Gifts to heart often give handmade or personal things, a letter, a meal, something they grew or wrote, alongside or instead of bought presents.
